usage: the room where you cook; everyday spoken word
장소 + 에서 for an action that happens there
the kitchen and the living room
examples: Mom is cooking in the kitchen.
에서 marks where the action happens
There is a refrigerator in the kitchen.
nuance: 부엌 is the warm, everyday word for the place where you cook and wash dishes. The more formal or apartment-brochure word is 주방, but in daily home talk people usually just say 부엌. Use 에서 for cooking actions and 에 for where things sit.
mistakes: Don't pronounce or spell it 부억 — the final letter is ㅋ (부엌).
Use 에서 for an action there (부엌에서 요리해요), not 에 (부엌에 요리해요 is wrong).

usage: the room with a bath/shower; 화장실 is the toilet
examples: I shower in the bathroom in the morning.
There is a towel in the bathroom.
nuance: 욕실 is the room for bathing and showering, often with a tub. In Korean homes it is usually the same room as the toilet, but 화장실 stresses the toilet and 욕실 stresses the bath. For asking where to go, beginners more often say 화장실; 욕실 sounds like the home washing room.
mistakes: Don't confuse 욕실 (bath room) with 거실 (living room).
When you mean a public toilet, say 화장실, not 욕실.

usage: a home room for reading and working
noun + noun shows whose room it is
examples: Dad reads books in the study.
There are many books in the study.
nuance: 서재 is a room at home used mainly for reading, studying, or desk work, usually full of books. It is not a school classroom (교실) or a library (도서관) — it is a private room in a house. If a home has no separate room, people just use 책상 in another room instead.
mistakes: 서재 is a home room, not a public library — that is 도서관.
Use 에서 for reading/working (서재에서 읽어요), and 에 for where things are (서재에 있어요).

usage: below ground level; opposite of 지상
examples: The storeroom is in the basement.
There is a mart on basement floor 1.
nuance: 지하 means the underground part of a building, the opposite of above-ground floors. With floor numbers it makes 지하 1층, 지하 2층 (B1, B2), which you see in apartments and department stores. On its own it often just means the basement of a home.
mistakes: 지하 is underground; the above-ground floor is 지상 or just 1층.
Floor numbering is 지하 1층 (지하 + number + 층), not 1층 지하.

usage: small room just under the roof
examples: There are many old things in the attic.
The children play in the attic.
The attic is a bit hot.
nuance: 다락방 is the small cozy room tucked right under the roof, often used for storage or as a hideaway space for kids. It usually has a low, slanted ceiling. The plainer word 다락 means the same loft space; 다락방 simply stresses that it is a room.
mistakes: 다락방 is under the roof; the basement below the house is 지하.
Use 에 with 올라가다 (다락방에 올라가요), not 에서, when you mean going up to it.

examples: I put the bicycle in the storeroom.
There is a lot of stuff in the storeroom.
nuance: 창고 is any space for storing things — a small home storeroom, an outdoor shed, or a big warehouse, depending on size. At home it is where you keep boxes, tools, and seasonal items. Use 에 with verbs like 넣다 and 두다 for putting things away.
mistakes: Use 에 (not 에서) with 넣다: 창고에 넣어요, not 창고에서 넣어요.
창고 is for storage; a garage for a car is specifically 차고.

usage: a space to keep a car
examples: I put the car in the garage.
There is no car in the garage.
nuance: 차고 is the home space made for keeping a car, like a garage attached to a house. The shared parking area for an apartment building is usually called 주차장 instead. Because 차고 and 창고 look and sound similar, keep them apart: 차(car)고 vs 창고 (storage).
mistakes: Don't mix up 차고 (garage, for cars) and 창고 (storeroom).
A large shared lot is 주차장, while 차고 is your own home garage.

usage: planted yard with flowers and trees
examples: I grow flowers in the garden.
에서 marks where you grow them
There are many trees in our garden.
nuance: 정원 is a planted, decorated garden with flowers, grass, and trees, giving a tidy, designed feeling. A plain open yard for everyday use is 마당, which feels more casual. Use 에서 for doing things there and 에 for where plants and objects sit.
mistakes: 정원 is a planted garden; a bare open yard is 마당.
Use 에서 for gardening actions (정원에서 키워요), not 에.

examples: The children play in the backyard.
There is a puppy in the backyard.
nuance: 뒷마당 is the yard behind the house (뒤 'back' + 마당 'yard'), while the front one is 앞마당. It is a casual everyday open space for kids, pets, and chores. Spell it with the sai-siot: 뒷마당, not 뒤마당.
mistakes: Spell it 뒷마당 (with ㅅ), not 뒤마당.
뒷마당 is the back; the front yard is 앞마당.

examples: I drink coffee on the balcony.
에서 marks where you drink it
There is a flowerpot on the balcony.
nuance: 발코니 is a loanword for an outdoor platform attached to a room, where you can stand outside the building. In everyday Korean apartments people often say 베란다 for a similar covered space, though strictly they differ. Use 에서 for actions and 에 for where things sit.
mistakes: Spell the loanword 발코니, not 빌코니 or 발코니아.
In casual home talk Koreans often say 베란다 for a similar space — they overlap but are not identical.

usage: the wall around a house or yard
examples: The cat is on top of the wall.
담장 위 = top of the wall
Flowers have bloomed on the wall.
nuance: 담장 is the outer wall or fence that surrounds a house or yard, marking the edge of the property. The shorter word 담 means the same thing. It is different from 벽, which is an inside or building wall of a room; 담장 is the boundary wall outside.
mistakes: 담장 is the outer boundary wall; a room's inside wall is 벽.
Both 담 and 담장 are fine — 담장 just sounds a bit more concrete.

usage: wood-floored open room in a Korean house
examples: Grandma is sitting on the wooden floor.
I watch TV on the wooden-floored hall.
nuance: 마루 is the open, wood-floored space in a traditional Korean home, often used like a living area where the family sits and relaxes. In modern apartments people more often say 거실 for the living room. Because you usually sit on it, 마루 pairs naturally with 앉다.
mistakes: 마루 is the wood-floored hall; the modern living room is usually called 거실.
Use 에 with 앉다 (마루에 앉아요), not 에서, for the place where you sit.

usage: the raised step under a doorway
examples: My foot caught on the threshold.
The threshold is a bit high.
nuance: 문턱 is the small raised step or sill at the bottom of a doorway that you step over when passing through. It is a common spot to trip, so people often warn each other about it. The word is 문 (door) + 턱 (ledge), so it means the door's ledge.
mistakes: 문턱 is the bottom doorsill, not the whole door (문).
Use 을/를 with 넘다 (문턱을 넘어요) when you mean stepping over it.
